patient.name: Emily Carter
patient.chiefComplaint: Rapid breathing and feeling like she can't catch her breath

history.hpi: Patient was at work when she suddenly began breathing rapidly, reports feeling like she 'can't get enough air' and numbness/tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. Coworkers called 911 after she became visibly distressed. No known trigger identified other than a stressful phone call moments before onset.
history.lastOralIntake: Coffee approximately 1 hour prior to onset
history.events: Sudden onset of rapid breathing and perioral/finger tingling after a stressful phone call at work; coworkers called 911

scene.location: Office breakroom, patient seated in a chair surrounded by concerned coworkers
scene.bystanders: Several coworkers present; report she was fine until a phone call minutes before symptoms began
visualCues: Patient seated, breathing rapidly and shallowly
Hands showing mild carpopedal spasm posturing
No accessory muscle use or nasal flaring
Room and patient appear otherwise unremarkable

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 22-year-old female seated and breathing rapidly, reporting she can't catch her breath, with tingling around her mouth and in her fingers. She is anxious but alert and able to speak in full sentences.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Rapid, shallow, symmetric chest rise, no accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, strong and rapid
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities; mild tingling reported in fingertips, no true weakness
otherFindings: Mild carpopedal spasm posturing of hands
No fever, cough, or recent illness reported
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can't catch my breath — my hands and my mouth feel all tingly, I feel like I'm going to pass out."

transitions.condition: Crew performs a full assessment including vital signs, breath sounds, SpO2, capnography, and history of onset/triggers, then provides verbal reassurance and coaching while ruling out organic causes of tachypnea.

phases.name: Full assessment and reassurance provided
phases.description: Crew completes a full assessment to rule out organic causes of the rapid breathing, confirms clear breath sounds and normal oxygenation, and provides verbal reassurance and coaching to help the patient slow her breathing.
phases.triggerCondition: After confirming no signs of hypoxia, wheezing, fever, or other organic findings on exam and history, the crew recognizes an anxiety-driven hyperventilation episode and shifts to non-pharmacologic reassurance and coaching.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Rapid but improving, symmetric, clear bilaterally
otherFindings: Breath sounds clear bilaterally, no wheeze
No fever, no cough, no recent illness
Patient beginning to follow coached breathing pattern
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Okay... I'm trying to breathe slower like you said."

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain full vital signs, SpO2, and waveform capnography to rule out hypoxia or true respiratory pathology
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Full set of vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment), temperature, and O2 saturation. Consider temperature and waveform capnography
expectedActions.rationale: Objective data is required before attributing tachypnea to anxiety.

expectedActions.shortAction: Auscultate breath sounds and assess air entry; confirm clear, symmetric, no wheeze
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Air entry (normal vs. diminished, prolonged expiratory phase) Breath sounds (wheezes, crackles, rales, rhonchi, diminished, clear)
expectedActions.rationale: Rules out bronchospasm or other organic causes of rapid breathing.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain focused history: onset, triggers, and concurrent symptoms to identify a psychogenic cause
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Onset of symptoms Concurrent symptoms (e.g., fever, cough, rhinorrhea, tongue/lip swelling, rash, labored breathing, foreign body aspiration) Usual triggers of symptoms (e.g., cigarette smoke, change in weather, upper respiratory infections, exercise)
expectedActions.rationale: A clear psychological trigger with no red-flag symptoms supports an anxiety etiology.

expectedActions.shortAction: Provide verbal reassurance and coached breathing; place patient in position of comfort
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Placement of the patient in a position of comfort ... Verbal reassurance to control anxiety
expectedActions.rationale: Non-pharmacologic coaching is the primary BLS intervention for anxiety-driven hyperventilation.

transitions.condition: With coaching, reassurance, and confirmation of normal exam findings, the patient's respiratory rate and heart rate normalize and tingling resolves.
Crew attributes the rapid breathing to anxiety without performing breath sound auscultation or SpO2/capnography trending; an evolving true respiratory process goes unrecognized.

phases.name: Breathing slows, symptoms resolve
phases.description: With reassurance and coaching, the patient's respiratory rate and heart rate normalize, tingling resolves, and she is transported for further evaluation in a position of comfort.
phases.triggerCondition: Coached breathing and reassurance, combined with a reassuring exam ruling out organic causes, lead to resolution of the hyperventilation episode.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Normal rate and depth, clear bilaterally
otherFindings: Respiratory rate and heart rate normalized
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a lot better now, thank you for staying with me."

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and transport in position of comfort
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport in position of comfort and reassess as indicated
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms sustained improvement and documents resolution prior to arrival.

phases.name: Anxiety assumed without full assessment
phases.description: The crew labels the episode as anxiety without auscultating breath sounds or trending SpO2/capnography. An evolving mild bronchospasm goes unrecognized as oxygenation begins to decline.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew attributes the rapid breathing to anxiety without performing breath sound auscultation or SpO2/capnography trending; an evolving true respiratory process goes unrecognized.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Rapid, new mild wheeze on exhalation not yet recognized
otherFindings: SpO2 trending down, not yet reassessed
Mild expiratory wheeze now present but not auscultated

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize incomplete assessment; auscultate breath sounds and reassess SpO2 for true hypoxia/wheeze
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Signs of distress include: Apprehension, anxiety, combativeness Hypoxia (less than 90% oxygen saturation)
expectedActions.rationale: A worsening exam signals a real respiratory process was missed under the anxiety assumption.
